title: Retrieval Eval: Recall@k and MRR
statement:
You changed the retriever behind a knowledge-base assistant. Before you ship it, you run it on a golden set: questions where a person has marked which documents are relevant. Two numbers tell you if it got better.

Write def solution(results, golden, k). results maps each query string to the list of doc ids the retriever returned, best first (ids in one list are distinct). golden maps each query to a non-empty list of distinct relevant doc ids.

  • recall@k for a query = (number of relevant ids among the first k results) / (number of relevant ids).
  • reciprocal rank for a query = 1 / rank of the first relevant id in the whole result list, with ranks starting at 1; 0 if no relevant id appears.

Average each metric over the queries in golden. A golden query missing from results retrieved nothing and scores 0 on both. Queries that appear only in results are ignored. The average reciprocal rank is the MRR (mean reciprocal rank).

Return [recall_at_k, mrr], each rounded with round(x, 3). If golden is empty, return [0.0, 0.0].

examples.why: q1: the top 2 are d3, d1; 1 of 2 relevant ids is there, recall 0.5; first relevant at rank 2, RR 0.5. q2: d9 is at rank 3, outside the top 2, recall 0; RR 1/3. Recall = (0.5 + 0) / 2 = 0.25. MRR = (0.5 + 0.333...) / 2 = 0.41666... → 0.417.
leave: recall 1, RR 1. budget: y is rank 2, so recall@1 is 0 and RR 0.5. payroll is missing from results: 0 and 0. Recall = 1/3 → 0.333. MRR = 1.5/3 = 0.5.

think.a: Recall@k asks "did the top k contain the relevant docs?" (the docs the model will actually read). MRR asks "how high was the first good one?" They disagree on purpose: a retriever can put one good doc first (high MRR) and miss the rest (low recall).

think.q: Ranked [x, a, b], relevant [a, b, c], k = 2?
think.a: Top 2 = x, a: 1 hit of 3, recall 0.333. First relevant is a at rank 2: RR 0.5.

think.q: What's the first thing you'd write?
think.a: Loop over results. That is the trap: a query the retriever dropped would vanish from the average and inflate your score. Loop over golden, the questions you care about, and treat missing results as empty.
"relevant ids among the results" → set membership. Turn each golden list into a set so each check is O(1), then one pass over the top k and one scan for the first hit.

1. If golden is empty, return [0.0, 0.0].
  2. For each golden query: relevant = set(...), ranked = results.get(q, []).
  3. Add hits / len(relevant) to the recall sum.
  4. Walk enumerate(ranked, start=1); on the first hit add 1 / rank and stop.
  5. Divide both sums by len(golden) and round to 3 places.

Empty golden set (division by zero). A golden query missing from results. An empty result list. A relevant doc at rank k + 1 (counts for MRR, not recall). k longer than the list. Extra queries in results.

hints: Iterate over golden.items(), not results, and use results.get(query, []) for missing queries.
Recall: sum(1 for d in ranked[:k] if d in relevant) / len(relevant). Slicing past the end of a list is safe in Python.
Reciprocal rank: for rank, d in enumerate(ranked, start=1): and break on the first relevant id. Guard the empty-golden case before you divide.
solution:
def solution(results, golden, k):
    if not golden:
        return [0.0, 0.0]
    recall_sum = 0.0
    rr_sum = 0.0
    for query, relevant_ids in golden.items():
        relevant = set(relevant_ids)              # O(1) membership checks
        ranked = results.get(query, [])           # a missing query retrieved nothing
        hits = sum(1 for doc_id in ranked[:k] if doc_id in relevant)
        recall_sum += hits / len(relevant)
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranked, start=1):
            if doc_id in relevant:                # first relevant doc only
                rr_sum += 1 / rank
                break
    n = len(golden)
    return [round(recall_sum / n, 3), round(rr_sum / n, 3)]
explain:
An eval is a loop over the golden set with two running sums. The judgment calls are in the edges, and those are what an interviewer probes.

  • Example 1, q1: ranked[:2] = ['d3', 'd1']; d1 is relevant, 1 of 2 → 0.5. Walk the list: rank 1 d3 no, rank 2 d1 yes → RR 0.5.
  • q2: ranked[:2] = ['d5', 'd2'], no hit → recall 0. Keep walking for RR: rank 3 d9 → 1/3.
  • Averages: recall 0.25, MRR 0.41666... → 0.417.

Say why both numbers matter: an assistant that reads the top 5 chunks needs high recall@5 to have the facts at all; MRR shows whether the best chunk lands where the model pays most attention. Run the same golden set before and after every retriever change, and look at the per-query rows, not only the average.
complexity: O(total result ids scanned + total relevant ids) time, O(max relevant ids per query) extra space

perf.label: performance: 1,000 queries, 200 results and 60 relevant ids each
perf.gen: [{'q%d' % i: ['d%d' % ((i * 31 + j * 7) % 5000) for j in range(200)] for i in range(1000)}, {'q%d' % i: ['d%d' % ((i * 13 + j * 101) % 5000) for j in range(60)] for i in range(1000)}, 150]

govtech.evidence: Practice shaped like the lab's public products (evals for GovBrain); not a reported interview question.
extensions: Return a per-query report as well, sorted by worst recall first, so you can read the failures instead of trusting one average.
Add precision@k and nDCG@k with graded relevance (golden gives each id a score 0-3). What does nDCG reward that recall ignores?
Compare two retrievers on the same golden set: list the queries where the new one is worse. With 50 golden queries, is a 0.02 MRR gain real or noise?

The golden set has duplicate query strings with different wording ("leave policy" vs "Leave Policy?"). Normalise keys before joining, and decide what happens when two golden entries collapse into one.
